stem: A client exposed to cold has a core temperature of 31°C (87.8°F), confusion, and slowed responses. Which management principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Encourage vigorous walking to generate heat and apply warming primarily to the hands and feet.
options.B: Handle the client gently, prevent further heat loss, use active external rewarming focused on the trunk, and continuously monitor cardiac status.
options.C: Massage the extremities vigorously and rapidly warm the arms and legs before warming the trunk.
options.D: Apply direct high-temperature heat to numb skin and defer cardiac monitoring until rewarming is complete.

rationale: A core temperature of 31°C is in the moderate hypothermia range. Current StatPearls/NCBI guidance states that patients with moderate or severe hypothermia should be moved gently because rough movement can increase myocardial irritability and precipitate dysrhythmias. Management includes preventing further heat loss and active external rewarming; efficient heat application is directed to the trunk, axillae, chest, and back, with continuous clinical and cardiac monitoring. Therefore B is correct. Vigorous exercise or massage and rapid peripheral warming can destabilize the client, and direct uncontrolled high heat risks burns and does not replace cardiac monitoring.
educational_objective: Manage moderate hypothermia with gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, trunk-focused active external rewarming, and continuous cardiac monitoring because myocardial irritability and dysrhythmias are important risks.
source_locator: Classification/clinical severity: moderate hypothermia is approximately 28-32°C. Treatment/Management: moderate/severe hypothermia requires gentle handling because rough movement can precipitate fatal dysrhythmias; prevent further heat loss; use active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia; heat packs/forced-air warming are applied to trunk/axillae/chest/back; maintain continuous clinical and cardiac monitoring; rapid peripheral warming can contribute to hemodynamic instability.
source_claim_supported: At 31°C with altered mentation, moderate hypothermia management includes gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, active trunk-focused rewarming, and cardiac monitoring; vigorous movement and aggressive peripheral warming are unsafe.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.46 and Medical Emergencies/Pathophysiology content: manage acute/life-threatening conditions, recognize complications, perform emergency care, and monitor physiologic responses to interventions.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — moderate hypothermia management and dysrhythmia prevention

source_original.stem: A client exposed to cold has a core temperature of 31°C (87.8°F), confusion, and slowed responses. Which management principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Encourage vigorous walking, warm the arms and legs first, and reassess after the client becomes more alert.
options.B: Handle gently, prevent further heat loss, actively rewarm the trunk, and monitor the cardiac rhythm.
options.C: Massage the extremities vigorously and apply peripheral heat to move warm blood toward the core.
options.D: Apply unmonitored direct high heat to numb skin and delay cardiac monitoring until rewarming is complete.

source_original.rationale: A core temperature of 31°C with altered mental status is clinically significant hypothermia. Care includes gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, active external rewarming focused on the trunk, and cardiac monitoring because dysrhythmias can occur. Option B is correct. Vigorous exercise, extremity massage, and uncontrolled direct heat are unsafe.
source_original.source_detail: Moderate hypothermia/management: temperatures about 28-32°C are moderate; handle patients gently because of dysrhythmia risk, prevent further heat loss, use active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia with heat directed to the trunk, and monitor cardiac status. Current StatPearls Hypothermia entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the moderate-hypothermia construct and key B, upgraded currentness to the June 21, 2026 StatPearls/NCBI update, and tightened the distractors around movement/peripheral-warming hazards. Reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a defined emergency management bundle.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current NCBI/StatPearls 2026 clinical guidance; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: StatPearls severity classification and Treatment/Management; NCSBN Physiological Adaptation
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses source-supported temperature classification, gentle handling, heat-loss prevention, trunk-focused active external rewarming, and cardiac monitoring. No unsupported rewarming rate or invasive modality is required.

distractor_audit.A: Vigorous walking/primarily peripheral warming is inappropriate for moderate hypothermia with altered mentation and arrhythmia risk.
distractor_audit.C: Vigorous massage and rapid extremity warming can worsen hemodynamic instability and do not reflect recommended trunk-focused management.
distractor_audit.D: Direct uncontrolled high heat risks tissue injury and delaying cardiac monitoring ignores dysrhythmia risk.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B combines all key moderate-hypothermia safety and rewarming principles without introducing a destabilizing action.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are rewarming/monitoring strategies; the answer is not identified by an unrelated diagnostic clue.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — environmental emergency management and complication prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the June 2026 StatPearls treatment section, temperature category, all options, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. B remained uniquely correct.
